blind_rationale: Marcillo, Krometis, and Krometis (2021) analyze Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) regulatory violations from 2006–2016 across N = 662 geocoded community water systems (CWSs) in Virginia (out of 1,133 state CWSs) by approximating service areas from 886 zip codes and linking 2000 US Census demographics, USDA RUCA rurality codes, and EPA SDWIS system attributes via LASSO-selected negative binomial regressions (Table 1, PDF p. 6). Evaluated blindly on its own primary research question and headline finding, the study is best classified as 'none_nonfit': (1) its primary tested exposures are sociodemographic environmental-justice predictors—specifically service-area %Black (Health-Based [HB] violations OR = 1.031, 95% CI: 1.018, 1.045; dropped by LASSO for Monitoring & Reporting [MR] violations), rurality (all RUCA categories null), and zip-code %Homeownership, which the authors explicitly operationalize as a Census socioeconomic status (SES)/wealth proxy because income and education were unavailable at the 2000 zip-code scale (main effects null: MR OR = 1.007, 95% CI: 0.990, 1.024; HB OR = 0.996, 95% CI: 0.966, 1.026; interaction with %Native Hawaii/Pacific Islander MR OR = 1.214, 95% CI: 1.013, 1.455, noted as a potential artifact since that group is 0.04% of Virginia's population)—rather than a legal tenure or eligibility rule governing household service connection (unconnected private-well households and deliberate historical service-boundary exclusions are omitted by proximity-based delineation, PDF p. 8); and (2) both outcomes are utility-level SDWIS regulatory compliance violation rates (MR administrative testing/reporting failures and HB MCL/MRDL/treatment-technique violations) rather than direct household water connection, continuity, or affordability. CRITICAL CONSISTENCY CHECK FOR PHASE 2: Table 1 also includes two institutional/system covariates—binary utility ownership ('Operation: Private [Reference: Public]', MR OR = 1.899, 95% CI: 1.455, 2.478, p < 0.05 [worse administrative compliance]; HB OR = 1.425, 95% CI: 0.837, 2.428 [null, directionally worse compliance]) and utility scale ('Size: Medium vs. Very Small', MR OR = 0.314, 95% CI: 0.148, 0.665, p < 0.05; dropped by LASSO for HB). If the extracted row in effect_sizes.csv is Private vs. Public CWS ownership (or CWS size), that exposure belongs conceptually to SWiM Family C (ownership, regulation, institutional capacity, administrative structure): excluding an MR-violation row as non-fit is substantively justified because failure to report/monitor is purely administrative utility compliance rather than household service access, whereas if the extracted row is Private vs. Public ownership on HB water-quality violations (OR = 1.425), exclusion would only be consistent if Family C also excludes other utility-level regulatory water-quality violation rows. Conversely, if the extracted row is %Black (fails narrow Criterion 2, E03) or area-level SES-proxy %Homeownership (proxy wealth indicator rather than a Family A tenure rule), non-fit / PI scope review is warranted.

headline_estimate_summary: LASSO-selected multivariable negative binomial regressions of annual/active-year-normalized EPA SDWIS violations (2006–2016) across N = 662 geocoded Virginia CWSs (Table 1, PDF p. 6; exponentiated coefficients reported as ORs with 95% CIs; SEs and exact p-values not printed, significance threshold p < 0.05; overall fit AIC = 8294, log-likelihood = -8237.99): (1) Primary demographic headline (%Black, per 1 percentage-point increase): Health-Based (HB) violations OR = 1.031 (95% CI: 1.018, 1.045; p < 0.05; raw OR > 1 indicates MORE HB violations = worse water-quality compliance), adjusted for %AIAN, %Asian, %NHPI, %Homeownership, %Age >= 65, %Homeownership x %NHPI, RUCA rurality, source water type, private operation, and year (excluded by LASSO from Monitoring & Reporting [MR] model). (2) Utility ownership (Operation: Private vs. Public reference): MR violations OR = 1.899 (95% CI: 1.455, 2.478; p < 0.05; ~90% higher likelihood of MR violation = worse administrative compliance), adjusted for %AIAN, %NHPI, %Homeownership, %Age >= 65, %Homeownership x %NHPI, RUCA, CWS size, and year; HB violations OR = 1.425 (95% CI: 0.837, 2.428; non-significant, directionally more HB violations). (3) Zip-code %Homeownership (SES proxy): MR violations OR = 1.007 (95% CI: 0.990, 1.024; null); HB violations OR = 0.996 (95% CI: 0.966, 1.026; null); interaction %Homeownership x %Native Hawaii/Pacific Islander MR OR = 1.214 (95% CI: 1.013, 1.455; p < 0.05) and HB OR = 1.198 (95% CI: 0.939, 1.528; null). (4) Institutional scale (CWS Size vs. Very Small [<500 served] reference): Medium (3,301–10,000 served) MR violations OR = 0.314 (95% CI: 0.148, 0.665; p < 0.05; 69% lower MR violation likelihood); Small OR = 1.048 (0.786, 1.397), Large OR = 0.488 (0.174, 1.365), Very Large OR = 0.132 (0.010, 1.703); Size excluded by LASSO from HB model. Year trend: MR OR = 0.928 (95% CI: 0.895, 0.963; p < 0.05); HB OR = 0.972 (95% CI: 0.910, 1.039).
study_design_and_sample: Observational ecological panel/cross-sectional negative binomial regression analysis (with LASSO variable selection) in Virginia, United States. Unit of analysis: geocoded community water systems (CWSs) with ArcGIS proximity-delineated zip-code-scale service areas, observed over 2006–2016 (including a linear Year covariate) and linked to area-weighted 2000 US Decennial Census zip-code demographics and 2004 USDA RUCA rurality codes. Primary analytic sample: N = 662 geocoded Virginia CWSs (delineated from 671 previously geocoded CWSs out of 1,133 total Virginia CWSs, spanning 886 zip codes and 134 counties/independent cities, serving >5.3 million residents or ~75% of Virginians on community water supplies).
